covered.why: Every interview opens with 'what is an agent' — must define autonomy, goal-directedness, environment interaction, and contrast with LLMs.
Core mental model for why LLMs can plan, reflect, and use tools; interviews probe limitations (no native state, no tools) and how prompting unlocks agency.
Standard discriminator — must contrast agents with chains, RAG pipelines, and single-turn prompting on multiple dimensions.
Foundational reasoning technique expected in any agent interview; basis for planning, reflection, and ToT/GoT.
Canonical pattern appearing in nearly every interview; must trace the thought-action-observation loop, prompt structure, and why it improves over zero-shot.
Universal requirement — interviews test schema design, parallel vs. sequential calls, error handling, and how tools extend LLM capabilities.
Key differentiator from simple tool use — interviews ask about hierarchical planning, replanning, and comparison to CoT.
Advanced planning variant — senior interviews ask when to use ToT vs. CoT, search strategies (BFS/DFS), and compute trade-offs.
Standard reliability pattern — interviews cover Reflexion, Self-Refine, and how reflection integrates with ReAct loops.
Frequent topic — must distinguish memory types, retrieval strategies (similarity, recency, importance), and context window management.
Practical integration — interviews ask how agents use RAG differently from static pipelines (active retrieval, tool-formulated queries, hybrid search).
Production pattern — approval gates, clarification asks, and interruptibility are common design questions.
Baseline architecture — interviews expect you to describe/draw a single-agent loop with memory, tools, planner, executor, and state management.
Major interview area — why use multiple agents, communication protocols, coordination challenges, and when not to use them.

covered.concept: Multi-Agent Collaboration Patterns (Debate, Hierarchy, Swarm, Sequential)
covered.why: Specific patterns interviewed — must compare debate vs. hierarchy, explain supervisor/worker, and name trade-offs (latency, cost, quality).
Dominant production framework — interviews ask about state graphs, checkpointers, human-in-the-loop, and why it replaced AgentExecutor.
Major multi-agent framework — interviews compare its conversation-centric model to LangGraph's graph-centric model.
Popular role-based framework — interviews ask about role/goal/backstory design, process vs. hierarchical processes, and when to choose it.
Historical context — interviews may ask why it was deprecated, what limitations led to LangGraph, or expect recognition in legacy codebases.
Microsoft ecosystem standard — relevant for enterprise interviews; planners, plugins, and kernel memory are distinctive.
Historical reference — interviews ask what they proved, why they failed in production, and what modern frameworks learned.
Growing interview topic — how to evaluate non-deterministic agents, offline vs. online eval, LLM-as-judge, trajectory evaluation.

covered.concept: Agent Benchmarks (AgentBench, WebShop, ALFWorld, τ-bench, GAIA, SWE-bench)
covered.why: Expected literacy — senior interviews ask which benchmark tests what (web nav, coding, reasoning), and limitations of each.

covered.concept: Failure Modes (Hallucination, Tool Errors, Planning Failures, Loops, Cost/Latency)
covered.why: Practical reliability — interviews probe debugging stories, loop detection, cost control, and mitigation strategies.
Production requirement — input/output guards, tool confirmation, sandboxing, and policy enforcement are standard topics.
Rapidly adopted standard — interviews increasingly ask about MCP servers, resource vs. tool vs. prompt, and integration patterns.
Emerging interoperability standard — Google-led; interviews test awareness of agent discovery, task negotiation, and cross-framework communication.
Practical API knowledge — interviews expect familiarity with JSON schema differences, parallel calling, and structured output modes.
Operational competence — traces, spans, token accounting, and replay debugging are expected for senior roles.

modules.title: Foundations & Core Mental Models
modules.capability: Explain what an agent is (autonomy, goal-directedness, environment interaction), why LLMs serve as reasoning engines and their limitations, distinguish agentic systems from chains/RAG/single-turn prompting, and describe chain-of-thought reasoning and its role in agentic behavior — using the precise terminology interviewers expect.
modules.why_here: These four concepts form the shared mental model every agentic AI interview assumes. They define what an agent is, why LLMs can drive one, how to distinguish agentic from non-agentic systems, and the foundational reasoning technique (CoT) that all patterns build on.

modules.title: Core Agentic Patterns
modules.capability: Compare and contrast the major single-agent patterns (ReAct, tool use, planning, ToT/GoT, reflection, memory, RAG-for-agents, human-in-the-loop), explain the prompt structure and control flow of each, describe when each pattern applies and how they compose (e.g., ReAct with memory, planning with reflection), and identify the characteristic failure modes interviewers probe.
modules.why_here: These eight patterns constitute the complete single-agent repertoire. Each extends the foundation with a distinct capability (acting, planning, searching, correcting, remembering, retrieving knowledge, involving humans). Interviews test them comparatively — when to use which, how they compose, and their failure modes.

modules.title: Agent Architectures
covers: Multi-Agent Collaboration Patterns (Debate, Hierarchy, Swarm, Sequential)
modules.capability: Diagram and explain a single-agent architecture (loop, memory, tools, planner, executor, state), describe why and when to introduce multiple agents, compare the four collaboration patterns (debate, hierarchy, swarm, sequential) on latency, cost, quality, and complexity, and justify an architectural choice for a given problem scenario.
modules.why_here: Architectures compose patterns into runnable systems. Single-agent architecture is the baseline; multi-agent systems and their collaboration patterns (debate, hierarchy, swarm, sequential) are the other major interview axis. These three concepts are always discussed together — coordination, communication, and topology.

modules.title: Frameworks & Implementation
modules.capability: Compare the major agentic frameworks (LangGraph, AutoGen, CrewAI, Semantic Kernel) on programming model (state graph vs. conversation vs. role-based vs. planner/plugin), explain why LangGraph replaced AgentExecutor, describe what AutoGPT/BabyAGI demonstrated and why they failed in production, and articulate the criteria for choosing a framework in a given context.
modules.why_here: Frameworks map patterns and architectures to production code. LangGraph (graph-centric), AutoGen (conversation-centric), CrewAI (role-centric), and Semantic Kernel (planner/plugin-centric) represent four distinct programming models. Legacy LangChain and AutoGPT/BabyAGI provide the historical contrast interviews expect.

Evaluation methodologies and benchmarks measure quality; failure modes, guardrails, and observability ensure reliability; MCP, A2A, and function calling standards enable interoperability. They share a concern: moving from prototype to production.
